fixes.explanation: David, king of Israel (2 Samuel 5:3), doesn't hand God a resume. He says, “…for no one alive is righteous before You.” That covers every living person, friend, and he doesn't leave himself out. I think it takes a big heart to walk into a prayer with no bragging at all.

A cave is a good guess, since David hid in some in other stories (1 Samuel 22:1), but this psalm doesn't mention one. What it says is darkness. The enemy has David “…dwell in darkness like those long since dead.” The verse describes how it feels, and it never names a place on a map.

David says, “I consider the work of Your hands.” He also says he remembers the days of old and meditates on all God's works. When he's low, he looks back at what God has done. Good habit, friend. It's like rereading the best batch notes when the oven's acting up.
The psalm doesn't go to any battles, friend. He says, “I meditate on all Your works; I consider the work of Your hands.” His eyes are on what God has done. His own highlight reel stays in the drawer.

David asks, “Do not hide Your face from me, or I will be like those who descend to the Pit.” He's saying how much he needs God to answer. The Pit is a picture of the grave, and that's the comparison he reaches for. I think this one is heavy, friend.

A sheep without a shepherd is a picture from other places in the Bible (Matthew 9:36), but not in this psalm. Here David says, “Do not hide Your face from me, or I will be like those who descend to the Pit.” Nothing in the verse mentions sheep. The picture is the Pit.

Grass that withers is a picture from other places in the Bible (Isaiah 40:7), but it isn't in this verse. David says, “…or I will be like those who descend to the Pit.” That's the comparison he uses. The Pit is his picture, friend.
David says, “I flee to You for refuge.” He's talking to the LORD, and that's where he runs. The enemy has pursued his soul, and he runs straight to God. That's a smart place to run.
Mountains show up in other psalms (Psalm 121:1), but not in this one. David says, “Deliver me from my enemies, O LORD; I flee to You for refuge.” His refuge isn't a place. It's the LORD Himself.

That's right. David prays, “May Your good Spirit lead me on level ground.” He's asking God's good Spirit to lead him. Level ground sounds good to me, friend. Like a countertop that doesn't wobble when I stamp.
David prays, “For the sake of Your name, O LORD, revive me.” The reason he gives is God's name. I think that's a big deal, friend, since it points his prayer at God and not at himself.
David's family doesn't come up anywhere in this psalm. What he says is, “For the sake of Your name, O LORD, revive me.” The reason is God's name, friend. That's the only sake he names.
David was a king (2 Samuel 5:3), so an army is a reasonable guess. This psalm never brings one up, though. He prays, “For the sake of Your name, O LORD, revive me.” His reason is God's name.
David prays, “And in Your loving devotion, cut off my enemies.” He's asking God to do it, and he asks it in God's loving devotion. This is a heavy line. He ends by saying, “…for I am Your servant.”
